questions.stem: The range of the dataset $4, 9, 2, 7, 15, 3$ is:
questions.explanation: Range $= 15 - 2 = 13$. It is the highest value minus the lowest value.

questions.stem: A small range indicates that the data is:
questions.explanation: A small range means the highest and lowest values are close together, indicating the data is consistent.

questions.stem: Why is the range considered a limited measure of spread?

options.text: Because it only uses two values and is affected by outliers
Because it is too difficult to calculate
Because it cannot be calculated from a frequency table
Because it is always the same as the mean

questions.explanation: The range only considers the highest and lowest values, so a single extreme outlier can dramatically inflate it. It tells us nothing about how the remaining values are distributed.

questions.stem: Two students have the same mean test score but Student A has a range of 8 and Student B has a range of 35. What can you conclude?

options.text: Student A performed better on average
Student B performed better on average

questions.explanation: Since they have the same mean, they perform equally well on average. Student A has a smaller range (8 vs 35), indicating more consistent performance.

questions.stem: If every value in a dataset is increased by 10, the range will:
questions.explanation: Adding 10 to every value increases both the highest and lowest by 10, so their difference (the range) remains unchanged.

questions.stem: A frequency table shows values from 3 to 7. The range is:
questions.explanation: Range $= 7 - 3 = 4$. Use the data values (not the frequencies) to calculate the range.

questions.stem: When comparing two datasets, you should always use:

options.text: Both an average and a measure of spread
Neither -- just look at the raw data

questions.explanation: To make a fair comparison, you need both an average (to compare typical values) and a measure of spread like the range (to compare consistency).
